 Screen Kim Ji-won plays a no-nonsense, miraculous surgeon in Doctor X: Mafia in White, our K-drama pick of the week
 By Ankita Chandra 
 Published: 9 Nov 2026, 7:31AM | 4 min read Kim Ji-won as Gye Su-jeong in Doctor X: Mafia in White
 Advertisement GENRE : Clinical drama, suspense-thriller 
 WHERE TO WATCH : Netflix 
 YOU WILL LOVE IT IF YOU LOVE:  
 Medical procedures 
 Individual against the system 
 Workplace controversies 
 Secrecy and suspense 
 Professional friendships 
 t2 RATING : 3/5
 The Robin Hood myth has shape-shifted through different centuries, settings and contexts without the least resistance because of its timeless balance of humanity at its brightest and darkest. For every individual who decides to build an equal and harmonious society, there is a massive maze of greed, selfishness and corruption to be braved. And vice versa. Netflix’s ongoing medical drama Doctor X: Mafia in White constructs a Robin Hood figure in a setting which perhaps needs such a figure the most: a hospital. It is a space where both miraculous recoveries and life-altering losses take place. However, with the current capitalistic set-up of elite healthcare chains, where hierarchical politics and professional egos can come between a doctor and their foremost duty to save lives, hospitals often become sites of corruption and exploitation.
 Challenging this ever-tangled maze of power structures is difficult in itself, and subverting it means compromising one’s career. But not so much for someone who has perfected her skills to the extent that no doctor in any department is a match for her spot-on diagnostic brilliance and surgical speed. Sounds like a fairy tale, but it is a ray of hope against the corrupt healthcare system that threatens the nobility of the medical profession. In Doctor X: Mafia in White , general surgeon Gye Su-jeong (Kim Ji-won) rises to the occasion. What makes things worse for her opponents is that she is not afraid of losing her career.
 The audience is reminded of the lingering trauma from Su-jeong’s past at the beginning of several episodes, as she stands in shock while a massive fire in a war zone burns many of her patients to death, some of them children. In the present, she is a lone wolf, a freelance medical professional who works for an agency that manages independent doctors. Su-jeong’s coping mechanism for keeping her trauma at bay is the act of “leaping before looking”. Unlike most seasoned medical professionals, who assess theoretical risks and the extent of damage a critical medical procedure may cause to their reputations, Su-jeong acts on mental calculations and diagnoses performed in seconds. She can also dash from one operating room to another, completing her own surgeries before arriving just in time to rectify another doctor’s potential failures. She knows her books like the back of her hand and possesses a keen eye for spotting hidden symptoms with an almost instinctual level of accuracy.
 Quite rightly, medical professionals in Korea have raised concerns over the unrealistic standards of diagnosis and surgical procedures depicted in the series, making Su-jeong’s story seem like a hospital fairytale in which the witchy godmother is a general surgeon who simply seems capable of performing any miraculous cure at the exact moment it is needed. It is not so simple in reality, and every little clinical procedure entails a long trail of legal and professional documentation, as well as elaborate negotiations across healthcare hierarchies. That, at least, seems to be what real doctors are saying.
 Ironically, that is exactly the point raised by the series, even if it compromises realistic representation to pose a more important, socially relevant question: Do abstract hierarchies and dry textual records really matter more than a life hanging in the balance?
 While the answer cannot be a complete rejection of authority, especially in healthcare, which is a pillar of life in every society, the series certainly offers a fresh perspective to start with. In an industry where doctors are under chronic stress from working overtime and constantly at risk of facing legal disputes and hefty repercussions every time they enter an operating room, providing ideal care and treatment without proper coordination and moral alignment is difficult. A lone wolf who defies authority because she is perfect at her job can provide a starting point, but hardly a solution in herself. Will the series offer a conclusive social message in its final couple of episodes? That remains to be seen.
 Characters we treasure... 
 KIM JI-WON AS  GYE SU-JEONG: A surgical superhero, Sujeong is a magical saviour in the corrupt medical circles of the hospital, where she arrives like cosmic justice. Ji-won, who has tackled multiple nuanced characters in shows such as My Liberation Notes, Queen of Tears and others, portrays Su-jeong as a powerful protagonist despite having perhaps the fewest lines to work with. With her silent, icy demeanour and no-nonsense approach at work, Su-jeong becomes a commanding force, standing apart from her self-serving colleagues.
 KIM WOO-SEOK AS PARK TAE-GYEONG: In a plot that relies heavily on the visual shock of operating-table scars and blood-soaked surgical gear, as well as the horrifying darkness buried within “angelic” healthcare professionals, Woo-seok’s character brings an innocent, sunshine-guy vibe. The actor plays Tae-gyeong, a young medical intern who becomes the audience’s moral compass in a show where every character harbours dark secrets. Taegyeong’s constant support for and faith in Su-jeong guide the audience towards recognising the divide between right and wrong in the complicated world of the healthcare industry.
